passage: Rohan, you cannot decide between commerce and computers? Let me tell you about a student I taught, Deepika. I am Chetan, her computer teacher. In the summer she signed up for a free coding course and a free beginner's accounting course, both online at home. Every week she wrote in a notebook which one she opened without being asked and which one she had to force herself to open. By the end of the holidays she had finished the accounting course, with all its small tests, and dropped coding at the third lesson. She showed me the notebook in July. It said what I could not have told her: she liked the ledgers. Her evidence was better than any advice I could have given.

qa.a: Deepika finished the beginner's accounting course.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel about each course, according to her notebook?
qa.a: She opened accounting willingly and had to force herself to open coding, so she enjoyed accounting more.

qa.q: What could Deepika do next with this evidence?
qa.a: Talk to an accountant or try a harder accounting lesson, because a further trial shows whether the interest holds.

qa.q: How might Chetan feel about the notebook?
qa.a: Impressed and a little humbled, since Chetan says the evidence was better than any advice.

grounding: A student takes an online coding course and an accounting course over the summer and uses which one she finished and enjoyed as evidence.
